sources.title: Yemen's government announces all-out war to reclaim land from Houthis
sources.excerpt: The Yemeni president's announcement comes amid an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition.
sources.text: Yemen's government announces all-out war to reclaim land from Houthis. The head of Yemen's internationally recognised government has announced it will wage an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis. It follows an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition in recent days. The Iran-backed group said it had struck sites belonging to Saudi national oil company Aramco, in response to what it described as 50 Saudi-led coalition strikes in 12 hours. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment. The Yemeni government's fierce statement was expected after the Houthis' offensive last month, which saw them seize control of the country's Red Sea coastline, including the vital shipping lane of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. On Sunday, Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address: "Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory." Yemen's capital, Sanaa, which has been held by the Houthis for more than a decade, has come under sustained attack as government forces try to weaken the group's military capabilities. Attacks on the Houthis have also spread across Yemen, including to the Saada region, the group's northern heartland. But security sources say the Iran-backed Houthis have continued to make gains. The frontline in Yemen remains focused around the key city of Taiz, which is still controlled by the internationally recognised government. On Sunday, the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the interim capital of the Yemeni government, AFP news agency reports. Citing three Yemeni military sources, AFP also reports that the Houthis now control the area and supply route, effectively encircling Taiz. "They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Chatham House think tank, told AFP. Al-Alimi was unlikely to have made the announcement without the green light from Saudi Arabia, which remains the key backer of his government. Saudi Arabia has been under constant attack as the Houthis try to target the country's economic lifeblood - oil. On Sunday, Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched a ballistic missile and drone attack on Aramco sites in the capital, Riyadh, and the oil-rich Khurais area in the kingdom's east. "Both operations successfully achieved their objectives," the spokesman said in a statement. "The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites." It is not the first time the group has said it has hit Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on Sunday's claimed attack, but has previously dismissed some claims as misleading, mocking the Houthis for "chasing imaginary victories". But it has once again shown the price Saudi Arabia - and, as a consequence, the global economy - could pay if it launched a new all-out war against the Houthis. In retaliation, Saudi Arabia has also been striking Houthi targets, according to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel. It said at least two people had been wounded in strikes on Sunday. On Saturday, Yemen's government also said its forces had hit Houthi targets across the country, including in Sanaa, Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the south-west. Yemen is one of the poorest countries in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis. A war erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital city from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of swathes of the country's north. Riyadh intervened in the war the following year, leading an international coalition. After several years of relative calm, the war reignited in July amid the widening conflict in the Middle East. Last month, a lightning offensive enabled the Houthis to seize the country's entire Red Sea coast, stopping Saudi Arabia from using it as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz. The strategy benefited the Houthis' main sponsor, Iran. But it has also forced Saudi Arabia back into direct military confrontation with the Houthis.

sources.title: Yemen’s Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi airports as conflict deepens
sources.excerpt: In a separate post the Houthis also said they targeted a military supply convoy near the airport in the Yemeni city of Aden, the interim capital for the government
sources.text: Yemen’s Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi airports as conflict deepens. In a separate post the Houthis also said they targeted a military supply convoy near the airport in the Yemeni city of Aden, the interim capital for the government. The Yemeni government's Saba news agency reported missiles and drones targeting that airport. The agency cited transport authorities as saying one of the missiles landed near the runway minutes before the scheduled arrival of a flight from Cairo, which was forced to divert to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia. Houthi drones and missiles also targeted Saudi Arabia's Abha airport and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, spokesman Saree said, claiming they had "hit their targets accurately". It is the second time this week that the Houthis claimed to have attacked the main airport in the Saudi capital. It is facing frequent temporary closures of its airspace, according to tracking website Flightradar24, but Saudi authorities have not publicly acknowledged the closures or confirmed any strikes targeting the airport. Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has been fighting the Houthis since 2015, and is now trying to roll back the group's latest advance. On Monday (October 5, 2026), the coalition said it was providing air support for the counter-offensive launched by the Yemeni government forces. After a four-year ceasefire, Yemen's civil war re-erupted in July. Last month the Houthis seized the entire western coastline along the Red Sea in the country's deadliest fighting in years. On Wednesday (October 7, 2026), new clashes in Yemen's west left at least 62 combatants dead, including 37 Houthis, military sources from both camps told AFP . The government's Saba news agency also said the Houthis fired a missile at the city of Taiz, which is held by government forces, wounding five civilians. "We went out into the street to check on the wounded and saw young civilians who had been hit. The Houthi shell landed in the middle of the street, right in an area crowded with civilians," Taiz resident Al-Fateh al-Eisaei told AFP . Yemen's government has announced a goal of retaking all Houthi territory — home to most of the country's population, and much of it held for more than a decade. The war has also caused a humanitarian crisis that has left most of the nation's population dependent on aid. The UN's International Organization for Migration on Wednesday (October 7, 2026) said more than 200,000 people have been internally displaced by the latest round of fighting. It also expressed alarm at the lack of funds available to counter the crisis in one of the world's poorest nations. sources.text: Yemen’s Houthis attack Aden airport as fighting intensifies. ⁠Yemen’s Houthis attacked Aden’s international airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones on Wednesday, the country’s transport ministry said, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi-backed government forces intensified. Fighting has been focused in recent days on areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the conflict between the US and Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz. This week, Yemeni government forces with Saudi-led coalition air support launched ‌a counteroffensive to recapture strategic territory near the strait and around the town of Mocha that the Houthis had captured in September, but it is unclear if their advance will hold. The fighting, a spillover from the wider US-Iran conflict, has revived a complex 12-year war in Yemen that led to one of the worst humanitarian crises globally and fragmented the Arab world’s most impoverished country. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted infrastructure including airports, oil refineries and pipelines in Saudi Arabia, a US ally. On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital Riyadh. It said it was tracking the launch platform over Houthi-controlled Sanaa and would destroy ⁠it, but gave no details of casualties or damage. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. ‌There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of an attack on the airport. Fighting on the western front remains concentrated in the Dhubab district overlooking Bab el-Mandeb, with pro-government forces attempting an advance in the strategic hills to the east of that coastal plain, Yemeni military and government ‌sources say. Fierce clashes have taken place, with the Houthis claiming they have repelled attacks. On Monday the Yemeni government said it had reached Mocha, which sits ⁠at a junction with a supply route ⁠to the critical battleground of Taiz, but the claim had been premature, according to Yemeni military officials on the ground and analysts. Hussam Radman, a researcher at the Sanaa Centre, a Yemen-focused think tank, said pro-government forces including the Giants Brigade, ‌a conservative Sunni Salafi group that has led the counteroffensive, were trying to take control of Dhubab and to advance in the mountains to its east. Control of those highlands would allow for government forces to more easily advance up the ‌rest of ‌the coast, he said. Along Yemen’s coast to the east, one missile landed near the runway at Aden International Airport minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, ‌the transport ministry said. Authorities cancelled the landing and diverted the aircraft to Jeddah, while two planes on the runway were moved away from the area over fears of further strikes, it ⁠added. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis. Aden International Airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control. The Houthis, who control much of Yemen’s north, ⁠seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia, fearful of rival Iran’s influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, to intervene. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted heavy fighting, but it did not lead to a lasting settlement. The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming, training and funding the ‌Houthis. The group, mountain fighters who have emerged as ‌a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones that threatens the region, denies being part of Iran’s Middle East proxy network, and says it develops its own weapons. Tehran also rejects the allegations. Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the southwestern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Saudi state television reported. In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had attacked Abha International Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait with ballistic missiles and drones. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm an attack on Abha airport.

sources.text: Iran-backed Houthis deny losing ground in Yemen as oil prices ease despite fierce fighting. Follow updates on the war in the Middle East for Wednesday, Oct. 7, here . Yemen's Houthis said Wednesday they had targeted King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital with a ballistic missile, the latest in repeated salvos aimed at the site. The strike was accurate, by God's grace, and led to a disruption of air traffic at the airport," said Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree in a statement on X. In a separate post, the Houthis said they also targeted military supplies at a camp area near the airport in the Yemen government's interim capital of Aden. The Houthis' latest claims came hours after the Saudi-led coalition backing the Yemen government said its forces had intercepted a ballistic missile north of Riyadh fired by the Iran-backed Houthis. The flurry of attacks was launched as the Houthis said they were holding their ground amid an onslaught by Yemeni government forces backed by the coalition's air power. Earlier this week, Yemen's military said its forces had uprooted Houthi fighters from the areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a Red Sea shipping chokepoint, and the port city of Mocha. Nicole M. Amor , was among those killed — said in a public Facebook statement Monday. "I am done asking quietly. Today, I am asking the American people to stand with these six families and demand transparency." Some Gold Star families say they are grateful for how the Trump administration and military have honored their loved one's sacrifice. Other families say the way the White House has handled the reception is the latest indication that the administration does not respect the price they have paid. The spouse of Maj. Alex Klinner, an airman who was killed in an Iran-related combat operation this summer, said receiving less than two weeks' notice did not give her enough time to arrange for overnight care for her three young children. In a text message, Libby Klinner said she would not have gone anyway, adding, "I have no interest in supporting an administration that has been so reckless with the lives of our service members." The war, launched Feb. 28, has claimed the lives of 19 U.S. troops and wounded more than 800 others. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. Joined by its Yemeni government allies, Saudi Arabia is leading a coalition to attack Houthi military targets in Yemen. Their offensive follows the government's announcement on Sunday, declaring a campaign to reclaim Houthi-controlled territories in the country. Fighting has been concentrated in a region near the southern tip of the Red Sea to prevent disruptions to oil and gas exports. sources.title: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control
sources.excerpt: In rare access to Yemen's conflict zone the BBC travels to the front line with pro-government soldiers.
sources.text: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control. "This is the first drone," said the soldier accompanying us in south-western Yemen. "It's usually followed by an attack." The buzzing sound overhead got louder as we took cover under the bushes, before climbing back into the vehicle and driving away. Within about 10 minutes, the loud thuds of strikes followed, one after another, though it was unclear where they landed. It is hard to tell where the front line begins in the mountains south-west of the city of Taiz. Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war. We travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where their control ends and no man's land begins, in order to see the fighting up close. Homes are scattered across the slopes, but many stand abandoned after families fled to escape the fighting. It is eerily quiet, no sound of the cars or motorbikes that are continuously whizzing through the city. All you can hear is the bleating of livestock and the sound of incoming and outgoing fire. "Two mortars landed here on my property," said Ali, sitting outside his home with a herd of goats, about 1km (0.6 miles) from the front line. He told me he had sent his children to a displacement camp because they could no longer cope with the shelling and gunfire. He had stayed with his wife and sisters to look after their animals. "I am terrified," he said, "but I have no choice, we will all go hungry without our animals and die anyway." He gave only his first name, fearful of repercussions if the Houthis take over the area in the days ahead. Contacts from the Houthi side have told us they are consolidating troops, preparing for a major offensive. When we asked government forces about this they said they are aware and were preparing too. At the closest checkpoint to the front line, we met some fighters who had just returned from positions high on the mountain, just a few hundred metres from advancing Houthis. One of them said the bodies of 18 government soldiers lay in an area his unit could fire across but not reach. Fighting around Taiz has intensified since the Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port of Mokha, 85km to the west of the city, on 10 September, after a ceasefire that had largely held for four years unravelled. The group took control of a swathe of territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait – a crucial shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia. This contributed to a rise in oil prices as fears rose of further disruption to supplies from the region. Taiz is Yemen's third biggest city and its cultural capital, and is home to close to a million people. It sits at a vital intersection between Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen and government-held ones in the south – and is hemmed in by front lines in several directions. Government forces hold the centre of Taiz, while Houthi positions lie to its north and east. The fiercest recent fighting has been on the western approaches, where the two sides are contesting high ground overlooking the city's route south. If the Houthis secure these areas, government forces could find it much harder to retake Mokha. We travelled to Taiz from Aden in the south, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based. About 30 checkpoints along the route marked stretches of road controlled by different commanders – a clear sign of the fractured make-up of the forces fighting on the government side. As we neared the city, ambulances began to pass us. We counted at least five within half an hour, heading towards Taiz's main hospital. It was clear that we were driving into a city at the heart of a brutal battle. We arrived after dark. The shops were lit, the restaurants were packed and children were playing in the streets. But every so often, other sounds broke through – the thud of shelling and the crack of gunfire from the mountains around the city. Taiz has been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen. Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons. Their main outside supplier is Iran, which has provided weapons, funding and military advice, according to Saudi Arabia, Western countries and UN experts. Iran, however, has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically. There have been persistent reports over many years of the Houthis recruiting child soldiers, and a government soldier told us he had faced them on the front line. "It's difficult to look at a Yemeni child and shoot at him. But then they are pointing the gun at you and you have to defend yourself," he said. The Houthis signed an "action plan" with the UN in 2022 pledging to end the practice. The BBC has also spoken to teenagers serving with government forces. Meanwhile a coalition led by Saudi Arabia is backing the Yemeni government, and providing it with weapons. The Saudi military has carried out hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions on the Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have launched drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia. In the evening, at al-Thawra hospital in Taiz, casualties from the front lines were being brought into an intensive care unit where every bed we saw was occupied. Some patients were fighters, others were civilians. Twelve-year-old Ghana Nabeel had been herding goats when shrapnel struck her head. Her family said an incoming Houthi mortar had landed nearby. sources.title: Iran-backed Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Aden airport
sources.excerpt: Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces have launched a major offensive to retake territory that the rebels seized along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
sources.text: Iran-backed Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Aden airport. CAIRO — Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen on Wednesday claimed attacks on military facilities and airports in neighboring Saudi Arabia as the escalation deepened the latest front in the Iran war and threatened a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, said on social media that the rebels launched ballistic missiles and drones in the attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, but did not provide evidence. Flights to and from the airport were briefly disrupted, according to Flightradar24, a tracking platform. Saree said Abha airport, a frequent target of Houthi drones and missiles, was targeted. The rebels also claimed to have hit an air base in the city of Khamis Mushait and two military bases, Najran and Asir. All are in southwestern Saudi Arabia and near the border with Yemen. The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile north of Riyadh. Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces in recent days have launched a major ground and air offensive against the Houthis in an attempt to retake territory that the rebels seized about a month ago along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Those positions gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping as they pursue a blockade of Saudi vessels. On Monday, officials said forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen recaptured several key areas around the strait. The fighting has since then centered in and around the crucial town of Dhubab, 30 miles south of the port city of Mokha, according to both the Houthis and the Yemeni government. Clashes were also reported in the district of Waziayah in southwestern Taiz province, which links Yemen’s mountainous highlands to the Red Sea, and overlooks roads to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis also said they launched a missile strike early Wednesday against Yemen’s port city of Aden, the seat of the internationally recognized government. An Associated Press journalist heard explosions around 2 a.m. (7 p.m. Tuesday ET). The rebels hit a military camp close to the Aden airport with ballistic missiles, Saree said. Security authorities in Aden said the Houthis targeted the airport with two missiles, with no casualties. The airport is close to the seat of government. “The targeting of this vital civilian facility represents a direct threat to the safety of civilians, passengers, employees and flight crews,” Aden police said in a statement. The attack on the Aden airport threatened “a humanitarian disaster,” as one missile hit close to the runway just before the scheduled landing of a flight from Cairo, the Human Rights Ministry said. Flight 603, operated by Yemen’s flagship airline, landed safely in Aden at 3:30 a.m., according to flight tracking platform FlightAware. The ministry said the missile hit as other passengers were waiting to board their flight to the Saudi coastal city of Jeddah. “The Houthis believe that they can maximize Saudi economic costs and compel Saudi Arabia to surrender to Houthi demands by striking civilian infrastructure, such as oil facilities and airports,” the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, wrote in an analysis.

sources.text: YEMEN EXODUS: More Than 200,000 Displaced As War With Houthis Explodes Again. More than 200,000 Yemenis have been forced from their homes by the latest round of fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, the International Organization for Migration said Wednesday. The displacement has accelerated rapidly as Saudi-backed forces attempt to reverse Houthi gains around Yemen’s western coast and the strategically critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis have responded to the offensive with ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones targeting Saudi Arabia and government-controlled territory in Yemen. The renewed warfare has shattered years of relative calm between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis and created another major humanitarian emergency in a country devastated by more than a decade of conflict. Aid organizations are warning that communities already suffering from food insecurity, disease and inadequate medical services are now being forced to absorb another enormous population of displaced civilians.

sources.text: Houthis. The Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah or Ansarullah, are a Zaydi revivalist and Shia Islamist political and paramilitary organization that emerged from Yemen in the 1990s. It is predominantly made up of Zaydis, whose namesake leadership is drawn largely from the al-Houthi family. The Houthis are backed by Iran, and they are widely considered part of the Iranian-led Axis of Resistance.
